name: Royal Institution glass furnace
summary: In 1827 a dedicated room and furnaces were set up at the Royal Institution so Faraday could run the Royal Society's experiments on better optical glass.
description: A dedicated experimental room and furnaces brought Faraday’s optical-glass experiments onto the Royal Institution premises, with Sergeant Anderson assisting.
tier_reason: An installation serving a particular research programme is fine detail, separate from general furnace technology. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.
why: British optical glass for telescopes was poor, and a Royal Society committee was formed to improve it by experiment.

date.basis: Faraday reports the room and furnaces built in September 1827; the surviving notebook is headed October 1827.

events.statement: A dedicated experimental room and furnaces brought Faraday’s optical-glass experiments onto the Royal Institution premises, with Sergeant Anderson assisting.
events.caveats: This is a particular research installation, not the invention of a glass furnace. The entire manuscript was not inspected.

evidence.supports: Move from the Falcon Glassworks and construction at the Royal Institution.

evidence.locator: MS/365 catalogue: description and notebook heading
evidence.supports: Surviving 1827 furnace notebook and drawing identity.

date.label: by 19 November 1829
date.basis: Faraday’s Bakerian Lecture begun 19 November 1829 reports experimental furnace operation after the 1827 build; use was earlier than the report, not necessarily on the lecture date.

events.statement: By Faraday’s 1829 lecture, the Royal Institution furnaces had been used continuously for the committee’s optical-glass experimental work.
events.population: Royal Society glass committee workers at the Royal Institution
events.caveats: The upper bound avoids claiming an exact first firing day; the use was for specialist research and does not imply a market or general industrial adoption.

evidence.supports: Dates the lecture and describes the room and furnaces built in September 1827 and continuing glass-making work.
